title: Public sector undertakings: why BMS opposes disinvestment
author: Editorial Desk
summary: What the 2021 public sector policy says, why BMS opposes the sale of profit-making and strategic enterprises, and what workers should ask whenever a disinvestment is announced.
body:
Public sector undertakings (PSUs) were built to take India into steel, coal, power, oil, heavy engineering, banking and insurance, at a time when private capital was scarce and the country wanted to build its own industrial base. Today the same enterprises are at the centre of a policy debate about **disinvestment**, **strategic sale** and **privatisation**. This post sets out what the Government's policy actually says, what Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) has argued against it, where BMS accepts the need for change, and what workers should keep in mind whenever a sale is announced.

## What the policy says

The Government pursues disinvestment through two broad routes, as explained on the website of the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM). The first is **strategic disinvestment**, in which most or all of the Government's stake is sold and management control passes to the buyer; privatisation is a subset of this. The second is the sale of **minority stakes** through public offers, offers for sale and buybacks, where control stays with the State and the aim is mainly to deepen the capital market and widen public shareholding.

The present framework rests on the **New Public Sector Enterprise Policy of 2021**. According to reports on its release, the Cabinet approved it on 27 January 2021 and DIPAM published it on 4 February 2021, following announcements in the Budget for 2021-22. The policy names a set of **strategic sectors**: atomic energy, space and defence; transport and telecommunication; power, petroleum, coal and other minerals; and banking, insurance and financial services. In those sectors the policy says only a "bare minimum presence" of existing public enterprises will be kept at the holding-company level. The remaining enterprises in strategic sectors may be privatised, merged with or made subsidiaries of other public enterprises, or closed. In sectors not classed as strategic, public enterprises are slated for privatisation or closure.

The policy also describes a decision chain. NITI Aayog recommends which enterprises to retain or divest; a Core Group of Secretaries reviews the recommendation; an Alternative Mechanism that includes the Finance Minister and the concerned administrative minister approves it; and DIPAM then seeks in-principle approval from the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs case by case. Some bodies are outside the policy, among them development and regulatory bodies, autonomous organisations, trusts, port trusts, the Airports Authority of India, and units serving vulnerable groups or farmers. Railways and India Post are also excluded because they carry commercial operations with a development mandate.

Later steps made the machinery more detailed. In May 2022 the Cabinet authorised the boards of public enterprises to propose and carry out disinvestment, closure of subsidiaries or units, or sale of stakes in joint ventures. DIPAM issued guiding principles on 14 September 2022, and the Department of Public Enterprises issued principles for closure on 31 October 2022.

## The BMS position

BMS has consistently opposed the privatisation of **profit-making and strategic public enterprises**. Its objections have been put forward in several forms over the years.

In January 2020, when the sale of Air India was under discussion, BMS argued that selling public enterprises does not by itself solve the Government's need for revenue, because the State keeps its social responsibilities after the sale. It pointed out that public money has repeatedly been used to rescue private businesses and banks, which in its view amounts to a hidden subsidy to private owners while losses are passed on to the public. It also noted that several private airlines have struggled, and argued that a public enterprise should not be judged by profit and loss alone, since an airline like Air India flies many routes that serve connectivity rather than profit.

In October 2021, days after the Government signed a share purchase agreement with Tata Sons for Air India, BMS announced a nationwide demonstration under its **Public Sector Coordination Committee**. The main protest was planned in New Delhi near the MTNL building at the CGO Complex, and public sector unions affiliated to BMS were to send a memorandum to the Prime Minister. The demands covered a halt to strategic disinvestment, privatisation, asset monetisation, corporatisation and strategic sale of public enterprises, with particular concern for Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited; no further rise in the foreign direct investment limit; no bank mergers; an end to commercialisation of coal; changes to the industrial relations codes that it considered harmful to workers; and full implementation of the revival package for BSNL and MTNL. BMS said it would wait for the Government to respond until the Budget Session before deciding on further action.

Behind these specific demands there are four recurring arguments:

- Public enterprises provide **employment with security**, along with reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other classes, which private firms are not bound to offer.
- They serve **national purposes** such as defence production, energy security and banking in remote areas, which a purely commercial buyer may not prioritise.
- Sales at low valuations **transfer public wealth** to private hands. A factory, a mine or a refinery built over decades with public money is a public asset, and its price should reflect that.
- After transfer, workers' **service conditions, pensions and bargaining strength** are at risk, because the new owner is not bound by the old expectations except to the extent that the sale agreement and the law require.

## What BMS accepts

BMS does not claim that every public enterprise must be preserved exactly as it is. Its stated approach to sick or loss-making units is that they need a turnaround, with workers taking part in the planning, and it has suggested **workers' participation and cooperatives** as an alternative to outright sale in some cases. The distinction it draws is between repair and sale: a unit that has lost its way should be repaired, not handed over.

The recent history of BSNL gives a useful example of what repair involves. According to reports, a package of about Rs 70,000 crore in 2019 was built around a voluntary retirement scheme, debt restructuring and monetisation of assets. A second package approved in July 2022 was reported at Rs 1.64 lakh crore and combined financial support, debt restructuring, viability-gap funding and administrative allotment of spectrum, along with the merger of Bharat Broadband Network Limited into BSNL. A third package of Rs 89,047 crore approved in June 2023 was mainly to allot 4G and 5G spectrum. In September 2025 the Prime Minister inaugurated BSNL's indigenous 4G network with 97,500 towers. Whether this effort has restored the enterprise to health is a separate question, but the example shows that the State can choose to rescue a public enterprise rather than sell it, and that doing so is expensive and slow. It is that choice that BMS asks the Government to make more often.

## The Government's argument

The Government's case is that disinvestment improves efficiency, raises resources for public spending, and reflects the view that the State need not be in business where private players can do the job. Minority sales are presented as a way of widening the capital market and giving retail investors access to well-performing companies. The 2021 policy also states that a presence will be retained in strategic sectors, and it lists categories of enterprises that fall outside its scope. These are real policy positions and deserve to be read in full, not through slogans on either side.

## What workers should watch

Whenever a disinvestment proposal is announced, a worker or a reader can ask a handful of practical questions. Is the enterprise in a strategic sector or not, and will a minimum presence be retained? Is the proposal a minority stake sale, which leaves control with the State, or a strategic sale, which transfers management? What does the sale agreement say about existing employees, their pay, pensions, gratuity and retiree medical benefits? Are contract workers covered, or only regular staff? Will the buyer be required to keep the work in the same place? Has the recognised union been consulted before the decision, or informed after it? None of these questions requires a particular political view; they are the questions that decide what happens to ordinary families.

## What remains to be done

Three things remain unfinished. First, the consultation between the Government and workers' organisations on individual cases is uneven, and BMS has repeatedly asked for it to be made systematic. Second, many public enterprises still need a credible turnaround plan, with clear targets and timelines, rather than a choice between neglect and sale. Third, the protection of workers in a transfer should be written into the terms of every sale, so that no worker learns about the consequences only after the deal has closed.

## In closing

Behind each policy phrase there are people: the welder at a shipyard, the clerk at a bank branch, the engineer at a refinery, the contract worker at a mine. When you read about a sale, ask what happens to the workers, and who benefits. That question is at the heart of the BMS position, and it is a fair question to put to any policy, whichever way one finally votes.
